FAST

LONDON/HONG KONG, Nov 4 : Cryptocurrencies briefly dipped on Wednesday as Democrats won majorities in both the Senate and House in the US midterm elections, a potential blow to an industry that has pushed for faster deregulation for digital assets. The sector has spent more than $300 million backing crypto-friendly Democrats and Republicans in roughly equal measure during the current and previous election cycles, hoping to pass legislation US crypto companies say will put them on a solid legal footing and allow them to thrive. Bitcoin briefly touched a six-week low before recovering to trade roughly flat by 0715 GMT at $78,070. Ether traded at $2,292, up just 1 per cent.  Bitcoin has fallen by around 41 per cent since hitting record highs above $122,000 in October 2025, bringing the value of the broader crypto market to around $2.61 billion, according to CoinMarketCap.

The market has lost some $300 billion in value in the last month alone, as deepening concern about future returns from AI and the strain of rising borrowing costs pushed investors into less risky assets such as government bonds and safe-haven currencies.  Sentiment has also been hurt by the $6 billion hack of the Binance platform last week, the largest heist in history.  On Tuesday, Binance customers had withdrawn a net $4.72 billion from the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange since it reopened following the hack at the weekend. "The market may be re-evaluating the risk-reward profile of crypto assets. On one hand, the string of security incidents is forcing investors to re-examine the industry's security infrastructure and custody risks," Tim Sun, Senior Researcher at HashKey, said. "On the other hand, potential shifts in the US political landscape could stall the progress of structural crypto legislation and institutional framework development. All of these factors leave the crypto market facing strong headwinds," he said. Trump, who vowed to make the United States the "crypto capital of the world" during his 2024 presidential campaign, has made his own forays into digital assets, with the launch of his "Trump" meme coin, plus his family's World Liberty Financial crypto platform, among other ventures. The sector has seen sweeping reforms in the almost two years since Trump returned to office, including lighter enforcement, the creation of a strategic bitcoin reserve.  Washington has also allowed for easier access to banking and exchange-traded products and passed a federal stablecoin law that could help these assets move into the mainstream payments and money transfer systems.

Source: Reuters

FAST

SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 3 : Advanced Micro Devices' strategy of offering stakes in its future success to major AI customers OpenAI and Meta Platforms in exchange for big chip commitments is beginning to leave a sizeable imprint on its profits. AMD in February agreed to sell up to $60 billion worth of AI chips to Meta over five years, giving the Facebook owner warrants that could let it buy as much as 10 per cent of the chip firm if it meets certain milestones. The deal followed a similar agreement with OpenAI last year, giving the startup the option to buy up to roughly 10 per cent of the chipmaker. On Tuesday, AMD said it recorded a $1.07 billion non-cash charge, or 66 cents a share, in the third quarter ended September 26 to account for these warrants, as shipments under the agreements begin to ramp up. The chipmaker forecast faster-than-expected 2027 growth thanks to surging data-center sales, sending its shares up 8 per cent in extended trading and pushing up stocks of Intel, Nvidia and Broadcom.

The warrants are part of a growing use of equity incentives by chip and AI cloud companies to secure massive, long-term purchases from a small group of AI customers, and highlight the circular nature of the AI boom, where companies can simultaneously be customers, suppliers and investors in one another. The strategy also risks diluting AMD shareholders. OpenAI and Meta could own a large stake in the chipmaker for as little as a penny apiece if the warrants fully vest and are exercised, potentially increasing AMD's share count substantially. The warrants' ultimate value depends on AMD's share price when they are exercised. OpenAI's warrant also includes AMD share-price thresholds, while Meta's does not. Analysts said it was a major vote of confidence in AMD's AI chips and software but is unlikely to dent Nvidia's dominance, as the market leader continues to sell every AI chip it can make. "While I do believe incentives played a role in some of their sales, I believe the bigger issue is that there is pent-up demand for a serious alternative to Nvidia and AMD’s products are now starting to compete on price/performance metrics," TECHnalysis Research chief analyst Bob O'Donnell said. AMD has also struck a chip-purchase arrangement with OpenAI rival Anthropic, but that agreement included a commitment by AMD to invest in Anthropic. AMD finance chief Jean Hu said on Tuesday's analyst call that the warrants would begin diluting AMD shareholders once OpenAI and Meta satisfy the vesting and exercise conditions, which include shipment and other commercial requirements. AMD expects to provide more guidance in 2027 on when those conditions could be met, she said. Other AI chip and infrastructure companies have struck similar equity-linked deals with major customers. Chip startup Cerebras granted OpenAI warrants against a $20 billion commitment, while Marvell has issued Alphabet's Google warrants that give the search giant the right to buy a potential $12.2 billion stake. Qualcomm gave Amazon warrants in a $60 billion deal for its AI data-center chips.

Source: Reuters

FAST

BEIJING, Nov 4 : Oil prices slipped in early trade on Wednesday as investors awaited the results of the US midterm elections and their potential impact on peace talks in the Middle East, even after industry data showed US crude stocks unexpectedly fell last week. Brent futures fell 26 cents, or 0.25 per cent, to $103.34 a barrel by 0157 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate crude futures fell 53 cents, or 0.55 per cent, to $95.56. In the previous session, Brent eased more than 1 per cent to its lowest level in nearly four weeks as traders weighed talks to end the wars in Ukraine and Iran. Vote counting was underway in the US midterm elections, which will determine whether Trump's Republican Party retains control of Congress for the rest of his second term.

Markets remained on watch for any progress in talks to end the US-Israeli war with Iran, as Qatar stepped up mediation efforts to avert an escalation of attacks after the US midterm elections. A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Tuesday that Iran and the United States remain far from a deal to end their war. The United States carried out "defensive" strikes on Iran's Qeshm island targeting surface-to-air missiles used against US assets, a US official said on Tuesday. Another official said the strikes appeared limited and did not signal a return to major combat operations. US President Donald Trump told the Financial Times on Tuesday that the United States had no immediate plans to strike Iran. “We seem to be getting everything we want,” Trump said in the six-minute telephone interview. Meanwhile, crude stocks fell by 5.27 million barrels in the week ended October 30, market sources said on Wednesday, citing data from the American Petroleum Institute. Eight analysts polled by Reuters had expected, on average, a rise of about 880,000 barrels in crude inventories. Gasoline stocks rose by 1.43 million barrels, while distillate inventories fell by 1.19 million barrels from a week earlier, the sources said. "Diesel inventories remain tight, while gasoline stocks rose more than expected. The data are broadly supportive of oil prices," Haitong Futures said in a note on Wednesday. Official data from the US Energy Information Administration is due at 10:30 a.m. EST (1530 GMT) on Wednesday.

TOKYO, Nov 4 : Japan Investment Corp (JIC), a state-backed fund, plans to sell chipmaking materials maker JSR to Mitsui Chemicals in a deal that could exceed 1.3 trillion yen ($8.20 billion), two people familiar with the matter said. A decision could come as soon as within the month, said one of the people, who were speaking on condition of anonymity. Mitsui Chemicals said it is considering various options including acquiring JSR but no decision has been made. JIC and JSR did not reply to requests for comment. A deal would reshape Japan's chip supply chain as the government seeks to improve its competitiveness even as market participants see it as a large acquisition for Mitsui Chemicals to digest financially.

Reuters, which previously reported JIC is considering selling JSR, is reporting the final buyer for the first time. Shares in Mitsui Chemicals fell 13 per cent following Reuters' report. JIC acquired JSR for some 900 billion yen two years ago and had said it planned to use the business to drive consolidation in the semiconductor materials sector. The fund will instead sell JSR to a domestic chemical major as it takes advantage of a lift in the valuation of chip-related firms due to a boom in AI investment. JSR, established in 1957, is a leading manufacturer of photoresists which are used to transfer circuit patterns onto semiconductor wafers. Mitsui Chemicals, which is also expanding its chip materials business, has a market capitalisation of about 800 billion yen, "Concern about the substantial amount of funding needed appear to have come to the fore," said Tsutomu Yamada, an analyst at Mitsubishi UFJ eSmart Securities, of the share fall. The deal could be among the largest in Japan's chemicals sector, exceeding the 2020 acquisition of Hitachi Chemical by Showa Denko which created Resonac Holdings. Mitsui Chemicals had 217.8 billion yen in cash and cash equivalents and 876.4 billion yen in interest-bearing debt as at the end of June. Its debt-to-equity ratio, a measure of financial soundness, stood at 0.75. "Adding JSR's semiconductor strengths could boost its presence in the sector and lead to a re-rating," said Yamada. Japan has many companies making niche but essential materials for the chip supply chain. "The materials market is getting bigger and bigger, particularly thanks to AI," said Akira Minamikawa, an analyst at Omdia. "If you remain small you're going to become unable to address that growing market." JIC, which is overseen by the trade ministry, was set up in 2018 to invest in companies with the goal of boosting Japan's competitiveness. Its investments include medical equipment maker Topcon alongside private equity firm KKR. ($1 = 158.5200 yen)

Nov 3 : Block on Tuesday raised its full-year gross profit outlook after strength in its Cash App unit lifted the firm's quarterly earnings, while also reaching a preliminary settlement with the US Department of Justice over its anti-money laundering program. Shares of the Jack Dorsey-led company rose 7 per cent in extended trading. The US economy grew at its fastest pace in a year in the third quarter, shrugging off higher oil prices due to the Iran war, signaling that consumers maintained robust spending, benefiting financial firms such as Block. Gross profit at Cash App, Block's consumer-focused financial platform, surged 27 per cent in the third quarter from a year earlier. Gross profit at its Square merchant business rose 14 per cent.

Cash App's growing banking and lending products have helped Block diversify its revenue streams beyond transaction fees. "We've seen continued strong spending on Cash App Card as well as strong repayment rates on Borrow, which for us are the signals that collectively tell us consumers are managing their finances and the strength of their pocketbook," Chief Financial Officer Amrita Ahuja told Reuters in an interview. But the diversification has also increased the company's credit losses. Block's losses on transaction, loan and consumer receivables rose 65.6 per cent to $601.7 million in the third quarter. Block now expects gross profit of $12.63 billion for 2026, representing 22 per cent growth, compared with its prior forecast of $12.51 billion. It forecast gross profit of $3.32 billion for the fourth quarter. The fintech firm also forecast 2027 gross profit of $14.52 billion, implying 15 per cent growth, as it expects AI investments to drive sustained growth. Executive Officer and Head of Business Owen Jennings said the company expects the fourth quarter to mark the first time it generates revenue directly from AI tools. Adjusted operating income rose to $923 million, or $1.13 per share, for the three months ended September 30, compared with $480 million, or 54 cents per share, a year earlier. REGULATORY OVERHANG EASES Separately, Block said it reached an agreement in principle with the US Department of Justice in October to defer for three years a charge that the company failed to maintain an effective anti-money laundering program in violation of the Bank Secrecy Act. The deferred prosecution agreement could result in an expected net payment of roughly $764 million after credits for prior regulatory resolutions, the company added. The disclosure removes some uncertainty related to the probe but the DOJ resolution remains subject to a final agreement and court approval, and Block warned the ultimate terms could result in losses exceeding the amount already accrued.

Source: Reuters

Nov 3 : Meta Platforms said on Tuesday it is raising $15 billion through a five-part US dollar bond offering, as the Facebook parent turns to debt markets to help finance accelerating investments in AI infrastructure. The offering adds to a wave of AI-related fundraising as companies seek capital for data centers, computing capacity and cloud expansion, despite historically relying on strong cash balances to fund growth. It comprises $3.25 billion of notes due in 2031 carrying a 5.85 per cent coupon and another $3.25 billion due in 2033 at 6.25 per cent, according to a regulatory filing. Meta previously tapped debt markets with a $25 billion investment-grade bond sale in April and a $30 billion offering last year, underscoring its growing use of external financing to fund long-term AI investments.

Meta has said it expects capital expenditure of $135 billion-$145 billion this year, largely driven by AI investments. Moody's assigned the new debt an Aa3 rating, saying it expects Meta to maintain conservative financial policies and a positive net cash position despite rising AI spending. Meta's total debt stood at $83.67 billion, as of September 30, according to data compiled by LSEG.

Nov 3 : Booking Holdings said on Tuesday it recorded a $900 million reduction in revenue and accrued a loss of $100 million related to an FTC action involving Priceline's connection to deceptive hotel ads. The company warned that its business could face further fines after the online travel agency's third-quarter revenue fell 1 per cent year-over-year as a result. Shares of the company were down 1.5 per cent in extended trading. The FTC has been investigating Priceline's relationship with Guest Reservations, a third-party website which often charges higher prices and fees for hotel rooms, and whether it violates a rule against impersonating other businesses, and other potential violations regarding fees. Guest Reservations has been the subject of more than 1,000 consumers' complaints to the Better Business Bureau, many of whom said they believed they were booking directly with hotels. Consumers complained of surprise fees and unresponsive customer service representatives.

Priceline, which is one of Bookings five consumer facing brands, supplies hotel room inventory to Guest Reservations through Priceline Partner Solutions, according to an ongoing lawsuit against the companies filed by San Francisco. In addition to the $1 billion cumulative hit related to the matter, a settlement has not been agreed and litigation remains possible, the company said in a filling. A settlement "would likely" include an agreement for Priceline to pay a certain amount to the FTC directly as well as to provide monetary restitution to certain US consumers, the company said. The company warned that future litigation and regulatory processes in other jurisdictions related to similar claims, could harm the company's business, results and reputation. An FTC spokesperson declined to comment. The company said it is in discussions with the FTC to resolve the matter. Reuters reported in October that the case could carry more than $500 million in potential penalties. The charge comes as global travel demand moderated toward the end of the third quarter, reflecting softer international travel trends, while domestic travel has remained resilient, Booking said in a statement on Tuesday. Travel disruptions to and from the Middle East and elevated airfares due to the conflict affected demand in October, alongside localized unrest in certain European cities. However, gross bookings grew 10 per cent year-on-year during the quarter and room nights grew 7 per cent, as the travel industry has been supported by affluent travelers. The Norwalk, Connecticut-based company posted a profit per share of $4.66 for the third quarter, compared with $3.98 per share in the year-ago period. Analysts were expecting $4.50 per share, according to data compiled by LSEG. Total revenue for the quarter ended September 30 came in at $8.89 billion, compared to about $9 billion a year earlier.

Nov 3 : AMD forecast faster-than-expected 2027 growth as its data-center sales surge and its multibillion-dollar challenge to Nvidia gathers pace, sending its shares up 8 per cent in extended trading. The forecast and market-beating third-quarter results offered a strong counterpoint on Tuesday to mounting fears that the AI boom is losing steam and soothed investor concerns after rival Intel issued a weak outlook last week. Intel's shares rose 2 per cent, Nvidia stock climbed over 1 per cent and Broadcom also advanced 1.2 per cent. On a conference call with analysts, AMD CEO Lisa Su said the company expects overall revenue to rise more than 80 per cent in 2027. Su's forecast is higher than the 77 per cent growth analysts estimate, according to LSEG data.

Su told analysts that 80 per cent of sales next year will come from data-center chips that will "drive the majority of our revenue and earnings growth." "We see demand across the data-center business, across our CPU business, as well as our data-center AI business," Su said. "And when you look at the rate and pace of that growth, we've been planning for it for the last several years." Data-center revenue jumped 97 per cent to a record $8.55 billion in the third quarter, exceeding estimates of $8.20 billion. The company expects fourth-quarter revenue of about $17 billion, plus or minus 3 per cent, above analysts' average estimate of $16.23 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG. AMD's line of chips is positioned to benefit from the massive AI data-center buildout, portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds Hendi Susanto said. "The stock's resilience despite broader pressure on AI-related names suggests investors see AMD's results as confirming its technology leadership and its strong position to keep gaining market share," he added. AMD is benefiting as a shift in AI workloads toward running models in real-world applications drives demand for its graphics processing units and central processors. "The AMD numbers provide a greatly needed boost both for AI infrastructure and even, to a smaller degree, the PC market," chief analyst at TECHnalysis Research Bob O'Donnell said. The company's adjusted gross margin is expected to be about 55 per cent, in line with estimates of 55.27 per cent and down from 56 per cent in the third quarter. RAMPING UP AI ROLLOUTS AMD has stepped up AI product rollouts, moving beyond standalone chips to compete with Nvidia's rack-scale systems. The company's flagship Helios rack, combining its MI455X accelerator and new "Venice" server chips, is in production and set for a larger ramp-up in the fourth quarter. The initial systems are being tested at Meta. AMD's third-quarter revenue rose 45 per cent to $13.38 billion, beating estimates of $13.09 billion. Adjusted profit came in at $2.09 per share, compared with estimates of $1.95. The semiconductor industry is also grappling with a global memory shortage, leaving expensive high-bandwidth memory used in AI processors in scarce supply as manufacturers race to increase production. Third-quarter sales in AMD's client and gaming segment, home to its PC chips and console processors, fell 8 per cent to $3.72 billion, missing estimates of $3.79 billion. AMD said it expects PC unit shipments to decline by a double-digit percentage next year, though Su said the company would "outperform the market." Last week, Intel forecast its chip revenue to decline in the mid-20 per cent range for its fourth quarter and the slowdown would last into 2027.

WASHINGTON, Nov 3 : The US Senate Commerce Committee will hold a hearing November 10 on President Donald Trump's nominee to serve on the five-member Federal Communications Commission that is considering the fate of Walt Disney's eight company-owned ABC television stations. In August, Trump nominated Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chair Brendan Carr, to serve on one of the two open seats. The FCC currently has two Republicans and one Democrat, Commissioner Anna Gomez, who some believe Trump might fire if his nominee is confirmed. The FCC historically is divided 3-2 with the party in control of the White House holding a majority. The law requires three members for a quorum. US law requires that only three of the five FCC commissioners can be from the same political party. Last month, Democratic US Senator Ron Wyden said that a 1982 law requires the FCC to have political balance at any operational size. If there are three commissioners on the FCC, only two can be from the same political party, Wyden said.

Trump fired two Democrats on the Federal Trade Commission and dismissed numerous other Democrats from other agencies including the National Transportation Safety Board, National Labor Relations Board and National Science Foundation Board. Some of those agencies are required by law to have commissioners from both parties. In April, Carr ordered an unprecedented early license review for all of Disney's ABC stations. The day before his order, Trump urged ABC to fire late-night host Jimmy Kimmel. Disney's stations' license renewals were not scheduled to be considered until October 2028. Before April, the FCC had not ordered an early review in more than 50 years. Disney has sued the FCC to block an early review of the ABC licenses and a US judge has not yet issued a ruling. Carr said last week he had not made any decisions on whether to seek to revoke them. At the Senate committee hearing, Severs is likely to face questions on the FCC's oversight of Disney as well as efforts to expand wireless spectrum and attempts by Elon Musk's SpaceX company to obtain wireless spectrum in order to compete with the three major US telecom carriers. Trump has repeatedly urged broadcasters to drop comedy or news programs he dislikes or which have been critical of his administration. He has pressed Carr to revoke licenses of broadcasters he finds unfair. In July, Trump called on the FCC to revoke licenses of Comcast-owned NBC and ABC for deciding not to air his remarks on election security on their broadcast channels. Broadcasters have broad First Amendment rights to make content decisions. Individual broadcast stations need FCC licenses to use public airwaves. While license revocations are exceptionally rare, critics say the prospect of losing a license can pressure broadcasters and raise concerns about government interference in editorial and programming decisions.

Nov 3 - US Senator Elizabeth Warren and four other lawmakers questioned McDonald's use of algorithmic pricing tools in a letter to CEO Chris Kempczinski, which the lawmakers shared with Reuters. The letter, dated November 2, cites a Reuters story from September 29 that found McDonald’s uses machine learning algorithms to generate what the company calls the “optimal price” recommendations for each menu item at each restaurant, based in part on an estimate of how much each store’s typical patrons are willing to pay. “We are concerned that McDonald’s may be using AI to squeeze consumers into paying higher prices, and that its AI pricing tools may facilitate collusion between franchisees who should be operating as competitors,” reads the letter, which was signed by Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, along with Democratic Representatives Greg Casar, Becca Balint, Jesus Garcia and Mary Gay Scanlon. The letter asks Kempczinski several questions, including whether the pricing tools use individual consumer data from McDonald's loyalty program, how franchisees might be encouraged to use the tools, and what antitrust review was done before the tools’ deployment. The lawmakers requested a response by November 16.

It also said its franchisees are free to set their own prices and that its pricing tools are “not a mandate.” The company also described Reuters reporting as “speculative and uninformed” claims that “attempt to recast a standard business practice as something controversial.” Three franchisees told Reuters for its September story that the pricing engine’s recommendations have widened price differences between nearby restaurants.  Two consumer class action lawsuits have been filed in federal court in recent weeks alleging the company illegally coordinates menu prices across franchisees and company-owned restaurants through a centralized algorithmic pricing system. "AI does not set the price of a Big Mac or any other menu item," the company said after the first suit was filed. Nov 3 : Dutch chipmaker Nexperia on Tuesday said it had launched legal proceedings at a Dutch court against its Chinese owner Wingtech and the company's founder Zhang Xuezheng. "The proceedings seek to hold the defendants accountable for actions that Nexperia believes have caused significant harm to the company and its business. Nexperia is seeking compensation for the resulting damages," the company said in a statement.

Source: Reuters
